transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi. Well, I guess I'm here because of my eating. It's just... what really scares me is that once I start eating, especially when I’m alone in the kitchen, it feels like I’ve stepped aside. I just can’t make myself stop even though I’m telling myself the whole time, ‘Janet, put it away.’ 

And I spend a lot of time in that kitchen now that I'm not working. I have my associate's degree, you know, and I used to work full-time, but being home all day is a big adjustment. The kitchen gets great morning light, though. We actually just painted it this pale yellow color—Buttercup, I think the shade was called at the hardware store. The guy behind the counter mixed it wrong the first time, made it look almost neon, can you believe that? I had to drive all the way back across town in traffic to get him to fix it. My husband said I should have just left it, but you can't have neon walls where you drink your morning coffee. 

But anyway, yes, when I'm in there by myself, it's like my brain just disconnects from my hands and I can't stop eating.
Can you describe what it feels like when you can’t stop eating? Do you feel like you’re not in control of your actions during those moments?

Yeah, exactly, it's just like I was saying. It's like I'm completely out of the driver's seat. I'm standing there, and my brain is literally screaming at me, "Janet, just put the box down, put it away," but my hands just keep going. It's like they have a mind of their own. 

Speaking of keeping my hands busy, I've actually been trying to take up knitting lately since I have all this free time now. My aunt left me all this beautiful yarn when she passed away last year. It's mostly this thick wool, which makes my fingers itch a little bit, but the colors are just gorgeous. She was such a talented knitter, she made everyone in the family these really intricate sweaters for Christmas every single year. I could never figure out the patterns she used, I think she got them from some vintage magazine she kept in her attic... 

But, um, what were we talking about? Oh, right, the control thing. But yes, I just feel completely powerless in those moments. I'm just watching myself do it, and no matter how hard I tell myself to stop, I just can't make it happen.
Can you tell me if these episodes where you feel out of control with eating happen regularly, and if so, how often do they occur?

Well, if I look back at my kitchen calendar, you know, where I write down my food bank weeks and everything... I'd say they've been happening most weeks. Usually once or twice a week, and it's been going on like that for many months now. 

Speaking of the food bank, I actually started volunteering there on Tuesday mornings. It gets me out of the house, which is nice, but they have us sorting all these canned goods and my goodness, the sheer number of expired cans people donate! Just last week I found a can of creamed corn from 2014. Can you imagine? I don't know why people don't check the dates before they drop things off. My husband says they probably just clean out their pantries and don't even look, but I always check the dates. I have this whole system where I rotate the cans in my own pantry so the older ones are in the front. I even bought these little plastic organizers from that home goods store down the street... 

But anyway, yeah, looking at the calendar, it's definitely been once or twice most weeks for a long time now.
Do these episodes where you feel out of control with eating cause you a lot of distress or interfere with your daily life in any way?

Well, it definitely upsets me. I mean, I still go to my volunteer shifts at the food bank, like I said, and I still go to these weekend craft fairs. I've actually been trying to sell some of the scarves I've been knitting with my aunt's yarn. I set up this really cute little table with a gingham tablecloth and everything. But, you know, the other vendors there are so chatty, and they always want to go grab a bite to eat together after we pack up. There's this little diner right around the corner from the fairgrounds that has these huge, fluffy pancakes. They serve breakfast all day, which my husband thinks is ridiculous, but I think it's charming. The waitress there, I think her name is Brenda, she always remembers my order... 

Oh, but what was I saying? Right, the distress. Yeah, so I've actually started making up excuses to not go to those shared meals with the other vendors after the fairs. Or even after the food bank shifts. I just... I feel so embarrassed about my eating, and sometimes I'm just so upset after an episode that I don't want anyone asking me what's wrong. I just want to go home and hide, honestly. So I guess it is interfering, in a way.
After these episodes where you feel out of control with eating, do you ever try to compensate by making yourself vomit, using laxatives, or exercising a lot more than usual?

Oh goodness, no. I could never make myself throw up, just the thought of it makes my stomach turn. And I definitely don't take any pills or laxatives or anything like that. 

As for exercising... well, my husband actually bought one of those fancy stationary bikes last year. You know, the ones with the big screen where the instructors yell at you to pedal faster? He was so excited about it, he set it up right in the corner of our living room. But you know how those things go, it basically turned into a very expensive clothes hanger within a month. I think right now it has three of my knitted cardigans draped over the handlebars. I keep telling him we should just move it down to the basement, but he insists he's going to start using it again once the weather turns cold. He reads all these fitness blogs online and gets these ideas in his head about winter training... 

But anyway, what was I saying? Oh, right. No, I don't do anything like that after I eat. I don't try to work it off or get rid of the food or anything. I mostly just sit there and feel awful about what I just did.

Can you tell me if there have been weeks where you had multiple episodes of feeling out of control with your eating, and has there been any week in the past three months where you didn’t have at least one of these episodes?

Well, like I was saying before, looking back at my kitchen calendar and my food bank weeks, it's pretty much been happening most weeks. Usually once or twice a week, and it's been going on like that for many months now. 

I actually had to go buy a new calendar for next year already. I found this beautiful one with pictures of different lighthouses from the East Coast. My husband and I went to Maine for our honeymoon, oh, it must be almost twenty-five years ago now. We saw the Portland Head Light, and it was just breathtaking. We stayed in this little bed and breakfast where the owner made blueberry muffins from scratch every morning. She said the secret was using wild Maine blueberries, they're so much smaller and sweeter than the ones you get at the regular grocery store. I've tried to recreate her recipe a few times, but it never comes out quite right. Maybe it's the oven, we have an electric one and she had this big, old-fashioned gas range... 

But, oh, right, your question. Um, yeah, looking at the calendar, there really haven't been any weeks in the past three months where I didn't have at least one episode. It's just been a steady once or twice a week for a long while.

latest_inference.note: The patient consistently reports recurrent episodes of eating with a sense of lack of control, occurring at least once or twice weekly for many months, with no compensatory behaviors. This supports a diagnosis of binge eating disorder (F50.2) or unspecified feeding or eating disorder (F50.0). Bulimia nervosa (F50.9) is ruled out due to the absence of compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, laxative use, or excessive exercise.

inference_history.note: The patient reports episodes of feeling out of control while eating, describing a sense of detachment and inability to stop despite internal resistance. These episodes occur once or twice a week and have been ongoing for months. The behavior causes significant distress and some social withdrawal, suggesting a possible eating disorder such as binge eating disorder (F50.2). Other differential diagnoses include unspecified eating disorder (F50.9), depression (F32.9 or F33.9, though less directly supported at this point), and adjustment disorder with mixed anxiety and depressed mood (F43.2) given the recent life change of not working. No clear evidence of an anxiety disorder primary to the eating behavior has been established yet.

Ruled out F43.2 (Adjustment Disorder with Mixed Anxiety and Depressed Mood) as the primary concern appears to be related to eating behaviors rather than a reaction to a psychosocial stressor. Symptoms continue to center around loss of control during eating episodes, frequency of these episodes, and associated distress, which supports the continuation of eating disorder codes. Further evaluation is needed to distinguish between Binge Eating Disorder (F50.2), Anorexia Nervosa (F50.0), and Eating Disorder, Unspecified (F50.9).
